summary:
With `t` team members, the final group occupies some arc of exactly `t` seats. Each swap can move one member
from outside into a guest's seat inside, so an arc needs as many swaps as it has guests. Slide a window of `t`
seats around the circle (indices modulo `n`) to find the arc with the most members; the answer is `t` minus
that. O(n).

question.md:
Seats form a circle; `1` is a team member, `0` a guest. Any two people can swap seats. Return the fewest swaps to
make all members sit together.

- **n up to 10⁵.**
- The first and last seats are neighbours.

**Edge cases to keep in mind**

- No team members, or everyone is a team member: 0 swaps.
- The best group may wrap around the end of the list (the table is round).
- A swap can move any two people, not just neighbours.

think.md:
**What does the final seating look like?** There are `t = 5` team members. When they sit together, they fill
some arc of exactly `5` consecutive seats, going around the table. So the question becomes: which arc should
they end up in, and how many swaps does that arc cost?

**Cost of one arc.** Inside the chosen arc, every guest has to leave, and outside it, every member has to come
in. The two numbers are equal (the arc has `t` seats and there are `t` members). One swap of a guest inside with a
member outside fixes one guest and one member, so the cost is exactly **the number of guests in the arc**; it
can't be done with fewer, because each swap moves at most one member into the arc.

**All arcs, by hand** (`seats = [1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1]`):

The arc starting at seat 0 already has 3 members, so **2** swap(s) are enough.

**Why a window works.** Arcs are windows of fixed length `t` over a circular array. Moving the arc one seat
clockwise adds one seat and removes one, so the member count updates in O(1). The circle is handled by letting the
index run past `n − 1` and taking `i % n`.

idea.md:
For every starting seat `i`, count the members in seats `i, i+1, …, i+t−1` (mod `n`). The best arc has the
most members, and the answer is `t − most`.

The reasoning about swaps is the important part; this approach then just evaluates every arc separately.

lines.text: `t` is the team size, which is also the length of the arc the team must occupy. `best` is the most members already sitting in one arc.

Each seat is tried as the start of the arc, including starts near the end whose arc wraps around to seat 0. Every index is tried as the left end of the window. Nothing learned from one start is reused for the next, which is exactly the waste the better approaches remove.
Count the members inside this arc, using `% n` to wrap around. Recounting `t` seats per arc is the slow part.
The guests in the best arc. Each needs one swap with a member outside, so this is the number of swaps.

complexity.md: **Time O(n · t)**, up to O(n²) when about half the seats are members. **Space O(1).**

Arc starting at seat 1: 3 guest(s) to swap out.
Arc starting at seat 2: 2 guest(s) to swap out.
Arc starting at seat 3: 2 guest(s) to swap out.
Arc starting at seat 4: 3 guest(s) to swap out.
Arc starting at seat 5: 3 guest(s) to swap out.
Arc starting at seat 6: 2 guest(s) to swap out.
Arc starting at seat 7: 3 guest(s) to swap out.

Arc starting at seat 9: 2 guest(s) to swap out.

walk.title: There are 5 team members, so the final group fills some arc of 5 seats. Try each arc and count the guests in it.

limits.md: Neighbouring arcs share `t − 1` seats but each is recounted: O(n · t), which is O(n²) when about half the seats are team members.

approaches.title: Circular sliding window

idea.md:
Count members in seats `0..t−1`. Then rotate the arc one seat at a time: seat `i % n` enters and seat
`(i − t) % n` leaves, for `i = t .. n + t − 2`. Track the largest member count.

**Coverage.** Starting seats `0, 1, …, n − 1` are each visited exactly once (the loop produces `n − 1`
further arcs after the first), including arcs that wrap past the end.

**Answer.** `t − (most members in an arc)` = fewest guests to swap out.

build: For `i = t .. n + t − 2`: `inside += seats[i % n] − seats[(i − t) % n]`; update `best`.

lines.text: Count the team. With nobody to seat, no swaps are needed. Returning early also avoids sliding a window of length 0.
Members already in seats `0 … t − 1`: the first arc, and the best so far.

Rotate the arc one seat clockwise. Seat `i % n` enters and seat `(i − t) % n` leaves; the modulo makes the arc wrap past the last seat. The loop runs `n − 1` times, so every starting seat is visited once.
Members missing from the fullest arc = guests inside it = swaps needed.

complexity.md: **Time O(n):** `t` for the first arc plus `n − 1` O(1) rotations. **Space O(1).**

steps.text: Window starting at seat 1: add seat 5, drop seat 0 → 2 members.
Window starting at seat 2: add seat 6, drop seat 1 → 3 members.
Window starting at seat 3: add seat 7, drop seat 2 → 3 members.
Window starting at seat 9: add seat 3, drop seat 8 → 3 members.
At most 3 members already sit together, so 5 − 3 = 2 swaps.

walk.title: Slide a window of 5 seats around the circle (index modulo n), keeping the count of members inside.

takeaways.md:
- **"Group k items together" → pick the window they end up in**; its cost is what doesn't belong there.
- **Arbitrary swaps:** each swap fixes one misplaced pair, so cost = number of outsiders inside the window.
- **Circular arrays:** run the index to `n + k − 1` and use `% n` (or concatenate the array with itself).
- **Pitfall:** forgetting arcs that wrap around the end.
